claims.text: The selected as-cast alloy is a near-equiatomic, high-configurational-entropy, single-phase BCC material.
High configurational entropy stabilizes a homogeneous BCC lattice.
High configurational entropy drives an atomically uniform distribution of elements.
A homogeneous BCC lattice optimizes the electron-phonon coupling.
Intermediate electron-phonon coupling in the homogeneous BCC alloy stabilizes conventional s-wave superconductivity.
Reducing the number of principal elements or making the composition less equiatomic reduces ideal configurational mixing entropy.
Lower configurational entropy degrades lattice homogeneity and increases local structural fluctuations.
Local structural fluctuations disrupt electronic-structure uniformity and reduce the effective superconducting pairing interaction.
The high-entropy variant will have a superconducting transition temperature near 7–8 K.
Related Nb-Ta-Ti-Zr-Hf high-entropy alloys exhibit a sharp transition to zero resistance and bulk diamagnetism near 7.6–7.7 K.
The high-entropy variant will have robust superconducting critical fields.
A related BCC Nb-Ti-Zr-Ta-Hf alloy has an upper critical field of 12.2 T.
Applying a magnetic field suppresses the superconducting transition temperature in a related alloy.
The lower-entropy variant will have a lower transition temperature, a broader transition, or reduced critical fields.
The proposed entropy-superconductivity relationship applies primarily to near-equiatomic HEAs with simple structures such as BCC.
Phase separation, secondary phases, or disorder beyond an optimal configurational-entropy window can invalidate the proposed relationship.
The quantitative changes in transition temperature and critical fields may depend on synthesis conditions.
Resistivity, magnetic susceptibility, and applied-field measurements can determine the transition temperature, bulk superconducting response, and critical fields.

contradictions.description: The experiment says the samples will have identical overall compositions except for configurational entropy, but the proposed way to change entropy is to remove principal elements, introduce a dominant component, or adjust elemental ratios. Those operations necessarily change overall composition, so entropy is not isolated from chemical-composition effects.

The mechanism predicts that reduced entropy increases structural inhomogeneity, whereas the experimental design says elemental mapping should ensure similar homogeneity in both samples. Confirming similar homogeneity would hold the proposed mediator constant rather than test its predicted change.
